Figure 1:From the official L3 harness to JustRUA.Left, every design we tested, by axis, with its score on the evaluation set, 111 episodes that cover all 42 tasks.
Right, the designs JustRUA keeps, in the order they were added.
Each bar is one evaluation-set run, the ring its first-round subset of 42 episodes, and the dashed line the cost of one first-round episode, a lower bound that assumes all cacheable input hits the cache.
Reusing experience draws on the tasks being scored, so none of its forms is kept, whatever the score.

Figure 2:The testbed loop and the four axes of the study.The model issues a command, the unchanged planner turns it into a motion, and the simulator returns the next observation and, at the end, the score.
Solid blue outlines mark the parts JustRUA changes from the official L3 harness, and each dashed area is one axis of the study.Table11in the appendix describes every variant on each axis.

Figure 4:Behaviours counted in the review, head camera, three moments of one episode each, from top to bottom.
Rings mark the object, or in the fourth column the free arm.
In the first column the gripper closes above a watch band and comes up empty.
The first three behaviours are failures and the last two are neutral.
Handovers through the table and unwanted contact are counted in the same way (AppendixE).

Figure 5:Motion length.The same 4.2 seconds oforganize_tablewithout the cap and with it, five head-camera frames each.
The trace below the frames is the movement in the head view, and each bar marks a stretch of continuous movement.
Without the cap, one unstable plan carries the arm across the table and in front of the camera before the model sees anything.
With the cap, every motion stops within 20 control steps, about 0.8 s.

Figure 6:make_kongwith a demonstration, head camera.
Top, four keyframes of the expert episode.
Middle and bottom, the same moments in our runs with the visual demonstration and with the text trajectory.
Both runs copy the handover through the table centre.
Neither copies the last step, where the demonstration grips the tile upright to push it into the row, and both knock the row over and score 0.

Figure 7:Predicted depth.(a) One head-camera frame with the raw Depth Pro prediction that the model receives, the same prediction scaled to the robot geometry and simulator depth, on a shared colour scale.
(b) Behaviour counts with robot readings only, with simulator depth and with predicted depth.

Figure 8:Four ways to present affordances, head-camera images of one observation ofinsert_tubesas the model receives them.
Yellow labels are grasp candidates with their approach direction, and blue, orange and purple shading marks surfaces the left arm, the right arm or both arms can reach.
(a) Marks drawn onto each camera view, with no depth image.
(b) Clean RGB and depth added back, so each camera appears three times.
(c) Predicted depth, with the clean RGB left out again.
(d) Clean RGB at full size and one panel that holds the six other views at256×192256\times 192pixels, with at most four grasp candidates.

Figure 9:Coordinate solving ininsert_tubes, head camera.
At its first decision the model casts rays from pixels of the left tube through the head camera onto the table plane, and its next command lands 1.2 mm from the solved tube axis.
At decision 15 it triangulates three holes of the rack and the tube tip from two cameras.
Bottom, the code of the first run and its output.
Distances compare the output of the code with the commands that followed, not with the true positions of the objects.
Two more cases are inFigure14.

Figure 10:One failure of each cause, three moments of the episode from top to bottom, with its first-round score.
Frames are from the head camera except where noted.
Inmake_kongone arm tries to flip the tile and set it into the row by itself.
Inpack_objects_into_boxthe dashed outline marks where the box stood before the arm pushed it.
Insort_nesting_dolls_by_sizethe doll slides out of the gripper as the arm swings.
Infasten_screwsboth pairs end up assembled, and the score stays low.

Figure 13:Visual demonstrationformake_kong, the 16 keyframes of the source episode, head camera, in reading order.
The model sees them once before its first decision.
Three tasks also include the author’s wrist-camera views.
No action trace or robot state is attached.

Figure 14:More coordinate solving.Top,fold_clothes. The model locates both cuffs on the table plane, and both hands then close within a few millimetres of the solved points.
Bottom,pick_from_conveyor_by_image. Two sight lines to the cup, from the head and the left wrist camera, meet at a height of 0.834 m, and the hand closes 1 mm from the solved rim.
Distances compare the output of the code with the commands and gripper positions that followed, not with the true positions of the objects.
